entity: South Carolina Chapter of Trout Unlimited
stance_basis: letter explicitly requests delay of licensing and states project will have significant negative impacts on water quality and aquatic community
summary: The South Carolina Chapter of Trout Unlimited submitted detailed technical comments opposing the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project, raising concerns about stream habitat destruction, siltation impacts on Howard Creek's trout fishery and spawning runs, degradation of Lake Jocassee's cold-water trout habitat, and inadequate flow augmentation mitigation. The organization argued that insufficient data existed to assess the project's full impacts and requested that licensing be deferred until ongoing studies were completed.
complaint_summary: The organization presents detailed analysis showing significant reductions in suitable trout habitat in Lake Jocassee over 1974–1975, argues that Bad Creek Project operation will remove cold-water inflow from the Whitewater River and further degrade the dissolved oxygen budget, raises concerns about turbidity impacts from reservoir bank erosion and borrow operations, and calls for rigorous studies of the zone of influence before impacts can be properly assessed.

statement.text:
Extensive valuer quality data supplied by the Applicant has been analyzed. Numerous meetings and discussions have also been held with representatives of Duke Power Company to review many questions raised by preliminary data previously available. It is assumed that the conclusions developed as a result of these meetings, which answered several of our previous concerns, will be presented by the Applicant and necessitate no discussion here.
Presented as Exhibit 1 are plots of suitable trout habitat for the months of July through October, 1974 and 1975. These plots were developed utilizing the habitat limits of 70° F. and both 4 and 5 mg/l dissolved oxygen. As can be readily seen from these plots, a significant downward shift in the depth of suitable habitat has occurred in the past year. Also evident is a reduction in the amount of suitable trout habitat during the successive years varying from less than ten percent in early summer to over thirty percent during late September. In addition, "suitable" trout habitat as defined by 5.0 mg/l D.O. disappeared beyond 7,000 feet during September, 1975. Utilizing the 4.0 mg/l criteria, less severe but still significant reductions and shifts in habitat are apparent.
No comment required.
Reductions in coldwater habitat in Lake Jocassee are discussed in revised Sections 2.2.2.2 and 3.2.2.3.

These shifts and reductions indicate that significant changes in the dissolved oxygen budget and temperature regime have occurred in the past two years. Since the operation of the Bad Creek Project will effectively remove the cold water inflow to Lake Jocassee from the Whitewater River by mixing, grave implications are raised over the fate of the cold water habitat.
The impact of project operation is discussed in revised Section 3 2.2.3.
The Applicant has developed data on the flows and water quality of the Whitewater River. By summing the historical inflows during stratified lake periods and assuming that this cold oxygenated water enters the lake hypolimnon (i.e. area of suitable cold water habitat), the resulting volume equals a layer of approximately two meter thickness over the lake. This oxygenated recharge to the hypolimnon is approximately ten percent of the suitable habitat. If construction and operation of the project are licensed, the resulting removal of this recharge will further reduce the already affected dissolved oxygen budget. Even more ominous are the implications of the further reductions from the future projects planned in the basin by the Applicant.
See preceding response.
The two years' data presented point to some complex factors of definition of suitable habitat and the causes for the observed habitat reductions. Studies are presently underway by the
See revised Section 9.2.

Applicant to perform additional dissolved oxygen and temperature measurements. Additional vertical netting studies are being carried out to determine the distribution of cold water fishes. These ongoing studies alone will provide the necessary data to truly define the limits of trout habitat and the changing dissolved oxygen budget of Lake Jocassee. Until these studies have been completed, no true evaluation of the potential negative impacts can be made by the Applicant.
No comment required.
The operation of the Bad Creek project will result in the discharge of water of generally poorer quality to a higher quality water of the main body lake. Both temperature and turbidity will be higher at times than the ambient lake quality. Temperatures will be higher much of the time due to the energy input as heat by pumping and generation turbines, friction in conduits, solar and air radiation and conduction in the reservoirs. During low flow periods in the Whitewater River, the cold water inflow will provide less dilution, thus accelerating the problem.
The impact of operation of the proposed project is discussed in Section 3.2.2.3.
Increased turbidity of discharged water and its effect on aquatic life have not been sufficiently addressed. The main contributor to siltation of upper Lake Jocassee will be the erosion of the Bad Creek Reservoir banks during rapid drawdown.
See following response.

Rainfall and wave action will erode the steep banks of exposed soil causing increased turbidity. Presented as Exhibit 2 are excerpts from the Soil Conservation Service Soil Survey of Oconee County. South Carolina, which indicates that soils of the project area are extremely susceptible to erosion. This is equally true when upper horizon soils are stripped during borrow operations and the weathered parent material is exposed.
Staff concurs. See revised Section 2.1.3.
The high flows discharged to the Whitewater River arm during generation will create a highly mixed state in the area. Model studies and calculations of mixing numbers indicate that substantial decreases in the extent of the zone of mixing will be achieved by construction of a stone fill weir downstream of the discharge point. Nonquantitative model studies support the conclusion that mixed water flowing over this weir would not mix vertically with the lake main body but would seem to push the mixed water zone as a wedge or front displacing lake water before it. While this evidence would indicate definite improvements in lake conditions with the weir, no quantitative evidence is available to define the extent of this zone of influence over the lake. The water of poorer quality discharged from the Project would appread over this undefined area of the lake, having effects on the total aquatic community. Without a rigorous definition of
Staff's analysis of the impact of the proposed weir is discussed in revised Section 3.2.2.3.

impacts associated with this project cannot be reasonably addressed.
The Applicant should perform studies necessary to define the extent of this zone of influence, nursery areas, fish migratory routes, benthic community, etc. This information is necessary to evaluate the degree of protection afforded the biological life of the reservoir and the extent of possible negative impacts.
See revised Section 9.2.
The area where the project will discharge is the relatively shallow cove of the Whitewater River. The diversity of fish and aquatic life is greater in such shallow areas. Fish spawn in these areas and their offspring use these regions as nursery areas. Prior to spawning migrations into tributaries, several species of cold water fishes concentrate in these areas awaiting optimal conditions for spawning runs. These shallow areas are normally more productive than deepwater due to more diverse substrates and more stable conditions due to lessened wave action and wind. The zone of influence of the project will impact a large lake area with its unique impacts. The turbidity releases from Bad Creek Reservoir, Whitewater River and adjacent land areas could impact the zone of influence in the following ways:
See revised Sections 3.1.2.3. and 9.2.

1. Decreased light ponetration with resulting decreased photosynthesis and primary food production.
See Section 3.1.2.3.
2. In high concentrations, physically lethal.
3. Smothering of sensitive benthic and fish spawning areas.
Extensive water quality degradation should not be permitted in the zone of influence due to the valued second-story fishery. Concentrations of turbidity, dissolved oxygen and temperature cannot exceed the values set by the State of South Carolina for Class A waters not should they exceed the 24-96 hour

 of any resident fish species.
